{{Short description|Prefix derived from numerals or other numbers}}
{{Redirect2|semi-|hemi-||Semi (disambiguation)|and|Hemi (disambiguation)}} {{use dmy dates |date=March 2024}}
'''Numeral''' or '''number prefixes''' are [[prefix]]es derived from [[Numeral (linguistics)|numeral]]s or occasionally other [[number]]s. In English and many other languages, they are used to coin numerous series of words. For example:

*[[triangle]], [[quadrilateral]], [[pentagon]], [[hexagon]], [[octagon]] (shape with 3&nbsp;sides, 4&nbsp;sides, 5&nbsp;sides, 6&nbsp;sides, 8&nbsp;sides)
* [[simplex communication|simplex]], [[duplex (telecommunications)|duplex]] (communication in only 1&nbsp;direction at a time, in 2&nbsp;directions simultaneously)
* [[unicycle]], [[bicycle]], [[tricycle]] (vehicle with 1&nbsp;wheel, 2&nbsp;wheels, 3&nbsp;wheels)
* dyad, triad, tetrad (2&nbsp;parts, 3&nbsp;parts, 4&nbsp;parts)
* [[twin|twins]], [[Multiple_birth#Triplets|triplets]], [[Multiple_birth#Quadruplets|quadruplets]] (multiple birth of 2&nbsp;children, 3&nbsp;children, 4&nbsp;children)
* [[biped]], [[quadruped]], hexapod (animal with 2&nbsp;feet, 4&nbsp;feet, 6&nbsp;feet)
* September, October, November, December ([[September (Roman month)|7th&nbsp;month]], [[October (Roman month)|8th&nbsp;month]], [[November (Roman month)|9th&nbsp;month]], [[December (Roman month)|10th&nbsp;month]]){{efn-ua|name=Roman Calendar|These months' prefixes originated in a conjectured, pre-historical Roman 10&nbsp;month calendar. See [[Roman Calendar]].}}
* [[binary number|binary]], [[ternary number|ternary]], [[octal number|octal]], [[decimal]], [[hexadecimal]] (numbers expressed in base&nbsp;2, base&nbsp;3, base&nbsp;8, base&nbsp;10, base&nbsp;16)
* Unary, binary, ternary, quaternary, quinary, senary, septenary, octonary, nonary, denary (related to having a certain number of something—parts, components, elements, divisions, etc.)
* septuagenarian, octogenarian (a person 70–79&nbsp;years old, 80–89&nbsp;years old)
* [[centipede]], [[millipede]], [[Myriapoda|myriapod]] (subgroups of [[arthropod]]s with numerous feet, suggesting but not implying approximately 100, {{val|1000}}, and {{val|10000}}&nbsp;feet respectively)

In many European languages there are two principal systems, taken from [[Latin]] and [[Greek language|Greek]], each with several subsystems; in addition, [[Sanskrit]] occupies a marginal position.{{efn-ua|name=Sanskrit|See [[Mendeleev's predicted elements]] for the most common use of Sanskrit numerical prefixes.}} There is also an international set of [[metric prefix]]es, which are used in the world's [[metric system|standard measurement system]].

== Table of number prefixes in English ==
In the following prefixes, a final vowel is normally dropped before a root that begins with a vowel, with the exceptions of ''bi-,'' which is extended to ''bis-'' before a vowel; among the other [[monosyllable]]s, ''du-'', ''di-'', ''dvi-'', and ''tri-'', never vary.

Words in the ''cardinal'' category are [[cardinal number (linguistics)|cardinal number]]s, such as the English ''one'', ''two'', ''three'', which name the count of items in a sequence. The ''multiple'' category are [[adverb]]ial numbers, like the English ''once'', ''twice'', ''thrice'', that specify the number of events or instances of otherwise identical or similar items. Enumeration with the ''distributive'' category originally was meant to specify ''one each'', ''two each'' or ''one by one'', ''two by two'', etc., giving how many items of each type are desired or had been found, although distinct word forms for that meaning are now mostly lost. The ''ordinal'' category are based on [[ordinal number (linguistics)|ordinal number]]s such as the English ''first'', ''second'', ''third'', which specify position of items in a sequence. In Latin and Greek, the ordinal forms are also used for fractions for amounts higher than&nbsp;2; only the fraction {{sfrac| 1 | 2 }} has special forms.

The same suffix may be used with more than one category of number, as for example the ordinal numbers second<u>ary</u> and terti<u>ary</u> and the distributive numbers bi<u>nary</u> and ter<u>nary</u>.

For the hundreds, there are competing forms: Those in ''-gent-'', from the original Latin, and those in ''-cent-'', derived from ''centi-'', etc. plus the prefixes for 1 through 9&nbsp;.

Many of the items in the following tables are not in general use, but may rather be regarded as coinages by individuals. In scientific contexts, either [[scientific notation]] or [[SI prefix]]es are used to express very large or very small numbers, and not unwieldy prefixes.

; Examples
{{notelist|group=examples|20em}}

== Occurrences ==
* Numerical prefixes occur in 19th-, 20th-, and 21st-century coinages, mainly the terms that are used in relation to or that are the names of technological innovations, such as [[Wiktionary:hexadecimal|hexadecimal]] and [[Wiktionary:bicycle|bicycle]]. Also used in medals that commemorate an [[anniversary]], such as sesquicentennial (150 years), [[centennial]] (100 years), or [[wikt:bicentennial|bicentennial]] (200 years).
* They occur in constructed words such as [[systematic name]]s. Systematic names use numerical prefixes derived from Greek, with one principal exception, [[Wiktionary:nona-|nona-]].
* They occur as prefixes to units of measure in the [[SI]] system. See [[SI prefix]].
* They occur as prefixes to units of computer data. See [[binary prefixes]].
* They occur in words in the same languages as the original number word, and their respective derivatives. (Strictly speaking, some of the common citations of these occurrences are ''not'' in fact occurrences of the prefixes. For example: [[Wiktionary:millennium|millennium]] is not formed from [[Wiktionary:milli-|milli-]], but is in fact derived from the same shared Latin root &ndash; [[Wiktionary:mille|mille]].)

Because of the common inheritance of Greek and Latin roots across the [[Romance language]]s, the import of much of that derived vocabulary into non-Romance languages (such as into [[English language|English]] via [[Norman language|Norman French]]), and the [[loanwords|borrowing]] of 19th and 20th century coinages into many languages, the same numerical prefixes occur in many languages.

Numerical prefixes are not restricted to denoting integers. Some of the SI prefixes denote negative powers of 10, i.e. division by a multiple of 10 rather than multiplication by it. Several common-use numerical prefixes denote [[vulgar fraction]]s.

Words containing non-technical numerical prefixes are usually not hyphenated. This is not an absolute rule, however, and there are exceptions (for example: [[Wiktionary:quarter-deck|quarter-deck]] occurs in addition to [[Wiktionary:quarterdeck|quarterdeck]]). There are no exceptions for words comprising technical numerical prefixes, though. [[Systematic name]]s and words comprising [[SI prefix]]es and binary prefixes are not hyphenated, by definition.

Nonetheless, for clarity, dictionaries list numerical prefixes in hyphenated form, to distinguish the prefixes from words with the same spellings (such as [[Wiktionary:duo-|duo-]] and [[Wiktionary:duo|duo]]).

Several technical numerical prefixes are not derived from words for numbers. ([[Wiktionary:mega-|mega-]] is not derived from a number word, for example.) Similarly, some are only derived from words for numbers inasmuch as they are [[word play]]. ([[Wiktionary:peta-|Peta-]] is word play on [[Wiktionary:penta-|penta-]], for example. See its etymology for details.) The [[metric prefix]]es peta, exa, zetta, yotta, ronna, and quetta are based on the Ancient Greek or Ancient Latin numbers from 5 to 10, referring to the fifth through tenth powers of 1000. The initial letter h has been removed from some of these stems and the initial letters z, y, r, and q have been added, ascending in reverse alphabetical order, to avoid confusion with other metric prefixes. 

The root language of a numerical prefix need not be related to the root language of the word that it prefixes. Some words comprising numerical prefixes are [[hybrid word]]s.

In certain classes of systematic names, there are a few other exceptions to the rule of using Greek-derived numerical prefixes. The [[IUPAC nomenclature of organic chemistry]], for example, uses the numerical prefixes derived from Greek, except for the prefix for 9 (as mentioned) and the prefixes from 1 to 4 (meth-, eth-, prop-, and but-), which are not derived from words for numbers. These prefixes were invented by the IUPAC, deriving them from the pre-existing names for several compounds that it was intended to preserve in the new system: [[wikt:methane|methane]] (via [[wikt:methyl|methyl]], which is in turn from the Greek word for wine), [[wikt:ethane|ethane]] (from [[wikt:ethyl|ethyl]] coined by [[Justus von Liebig]] in 1834), [[wikt:propane|propane]] (from [[wikt:propionic|propionic]], which is in turn from [[wikt:pro-|pro-]] and the Greek word for fat), and [[wikt:butane|butane]] (from [[wikt:butyl|butyl]], which is in turn from [[wikt:butyric|butyric]], which is in turn from the Latin word for butter).

=== Distributive Latin series ===
*unary, binary, trinary, quaternary, quinary, senary, ... vicenary ... centenary ...
*denarian, vicenarian, tricenarian, quadragenarian, quinquagenarian, sexagenarian, septuagenarian, octogenarian, nonagenarian, centenarian, ... millenarian

=== Greek series ===
* [[monad (disambiguation)|monad]], [[dyad (disambiguation)|dyad]], [[triad (disambiguation)|triad]], tetrad, [[pentad (disambiguation)|pentad]], hexad, heptad, ogdoad, [[ennead]], decad, ... triacontad, ... hecatontad, [[chiliad]], [[myriad]]
* [[digon]], trigon, [[tetragon]], [[pentagon]], [[hexagon]], [[heptagon]], [[octagon]], [[enneagon]], [[decagon]], [[hendecagon]], [[dodecagon]], ... [[enneadecagon]], [[icosagon]], [[triacontagon]], ... [[chiliagon]], [[myriagon]]
* [[trilogy]], [[tetralogy]], [[pentalogy]], [[hexalogy]], [[heptalogy]]
* [[monopod]], [[dipod]], [[tripod]], [[tetrapod]], [[hexapod (disambiguation)|hexapod]], [[octopod]], [[decapod (disambiguation)|decapod]]

=== Mixed language series ===
* [[pentane]], [[hexane]], [[heptane]], [[octane]], [[nonane]],{{efn-ua|In organic chemistry, most prefixes are Greek but the prefixes for 9 and 11 are Latin.}} [[decane]], [[undecane]], ... [[icosane]]
* [[binary number|binary]], [[ternary numeral system|ternary]], [[quaternary numeral system|quaternary]], [[quinary]], [[senary]], [[septenary]], [[octal]], [[nonary]], [[decimal]], [[duodecimal]], [[hexadecimal]], [[vigesimal]], [[quadrovigesimal]], [[duotrigesimal]], [[sexagesimal]], [[octogesimal]]
* The [[SI prefix]]es, ''peta-'', ''exa-'', ''zetta-'', ''yotta-'', ''ronna-'', and ''quetta-'', are based on the Ancient Greek or Ancient Latin numbers from 5 to 10, referring to the fifth through tenth powers of 1000. The initial letter ''h'' has been removed from some of these stems and the initial letters ''z'', ''y'', ''r'', and ''q'' have been added, ascending in reverse alphabetical order, to avoid confusion with other metric prefixes.
